title: The shared kitchen

context.situation: You share a flat with Roommate B. The kitchen needs cleaning. You both decide whether to clean it or leave it.
context.preferences: You both want a clean kitchen. Cleaning takes effort and nobody enjoys it. Cleaning while the other relaxes and still enjoys the clean kitchen feels unfair. Roommate B has the same kinds of feelings.
context.learnerControls: Only your own choice: Clean or Leave it.
context.opponentControls: Only B’s own choice. Neither of you can force the other.
context.knownUnknown: You both understand what is at stake for each other. You don’t know what B will choose.
context.timing: You choose at the same time. Neither sees the other’s choice.
context.payoffMeaning: Each outcome gets a number for each person on a 0–5 scale. A higher number means that person is happier with the outcome. Only the order and size within this situation matter; the numbers are not money.
context.task: Predict B’s choice, then make your own.

opponentPolicy.description: B’s behaviour in this exercise was fixed: 70% Leave it, 30% Clean. That behaviour is separate from the payoff structure of the game.
opponentPolicy.rationale: B mostly leaves it (Leave it gives B a higher payoff whatever A does) but sometimes cleans, as people often do. The mix makes both of B’s columns appear across attempts, so the learner meets the difference between a good decision and a lucky or unlucky outcome. It matches what A is told: A does not know B’s choice. The mix is an authored exercise rule, not a prediction about what theory says players will do.

prompts.decideNote: B is choosing at the same time and won’t see your choice.

outcomes.clean|clean: You both cleaned. The work was shared, and the kitchen is clean.
outcomes.clean|leave: You cleaned. B didn’t. The kitchen is clean, but you did all the work.
outcomes.leave|clean: B cleaned. You didn’t. The kitchen is clean, but B did all the work.
outcomes.leave|leave: Neither of you cleaned. The kitchen stays messy.

matrix.intro: Here is the whole game as a table.
howToRead: Each cell shows one possible combination of choices.
First number = your payoff. Second number = B’s payoff.
Your choice is the row. B’s choice is the column.

questions.prompt: If B chooses Clean, which is better for you?
If B chooses Leave it, which is better for you?
Looking at both comparisons, what pattern do you see?
questions.noneLabel: It depends on what B chooses.

feedback.bestReplyCorrect: {lines} Because B chose {opponentAction}, {best} is your best response. A best response is the action that gives you the higher payoff against what the other player chose.
feedback.bestReplyIncorrect: {lines} Because B chose {opponentAction}, {best} is your best response. A best response is the action that gives you the higher payoff against what the other player chose.
feedback.bestReplyTie: {lines} Both are equally good for you here.
feedback.dominantCorrect: {lines} {dominant} is a dominant strategy. A dominant strategy gives you a higher payoff no matter what the other player does.
feedback.dominantIncorrect: {lines} {dominant} is a dominant strategy. A dominant strategy gives you a higher payoff no matter what the other player does.
feedback.noneCorrect: {lines} Which is better depends on what B does.
feedback.noneIncorrect: {lines} No single action is better whatever B does; it depends on B.
feedback.bestReplyRepeat: {lines} Because B chose {opponentAction}, {best} is your best response.

closingNote: {dominant} gives each player a higher payoff whatever the other player does. If both choose {dominant}, both get {mutualYou}. If both choose Clean, both get {betterYou}. So each player’s individually better action leads to a result that is worse for both.
